card: Adds manual pruning and chainstate flushing to the libbitcoinkernel C API (btck_block_manager_prune_up_to_height and btck_chainstate_manager_flush) and enables kernel callers to open pruned datadirs. Currently, embedded kernel applications cannot open or manage pruned block directories (#35627). The PR refactors prune bookkeeping and file deletion out of validation flush logic into BlockManager, retaining blocks above the last chainstate flush fork point to guarantee recovery after unclean shutdowns. It depends on #36738 and #36854.
changed_since_previous: Now includes full diff context, verifying the internal refactoring of BlockManager prune limits and retry logic alongside the C API additions.
evidence: Addresses issue #35627 ("kernel: can't work with pruned blocksdir") and kernel-node/kernel-node#111
PR description notes: "The kernel can't open a data directory that a pruned node created, and it has no way to prune."

Commit d224fb8721 explains: "Files selected for pruning were kept in a local, so a failed flush left them on disk until the next startup. Keep them in BlockManager and delete them after the next block index write."
problem: Applications using libbitcoinkernel cannot open datadirs created by pruned Bitcoin Core nodes and have no interface to prune block and undo files. Additionally, block file deletion and prune bookkeeping were coupled directly to ChainstateManager's FlushStateToDisk, which prevented standalone block manager pruning and failed to clean up unlinked files after a failed flush.

risk.why: A flaw in prune height calculation or file deletion could prune blocks still required for chainstate recovery during a reorg or crash, causing database corruption or data loss on node restart.

scope_notes: This PR builds on unmerged refactors in #36738 and #36854 that extract block storage writing into BlockManager and make BlockManager independently constructible by kernel callers.
summary: Exposes manual pruning and chainstate flushing functions in libbitcoinkernel, enabling kernel users to open existing pruned data directories and prune block storage up to a specified height. It separates BlockManager lifecycle and storage operations from ChainstateManager, moving prune bookkeeping and deferred file deletion into BlockManager so pruning bounds safely preserve unpushed blocks required for crash recovery across reorgs.
